name: Classic-Style Test 1
source: Original questions written for LSAT Trainer in the style and difficulty of recent LSATs. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus: City planner: Some residents argue that Harlow’s downtown parking garage should be demolished because it is rarely more than half full. But the garage’s low usage reflects its high hourly rates, which the council set before the new transit line reduced downtown traffic. Lowering those rates would probably fill the garage. So the garage should be kept, at least until lower rates have been tried.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the conclusion drawn in the city planner’s argument?
choices: The garage is rarely more than half full because its hourly rates are high.
The downtown garage should not be demolished before lower rates have been tried.
Lowering the garage’s hourly rates would probably fill the garage.
The council set the garage’s rates before the transit line reduced downtown traffic.
Residents who want the garage demolished have misjudged how heavily it is used.
questions.explanation: The planner’s point, signaled by “So,” is that the garage should be kept until lower rates are tried, which is (B). (C) is the tempting choice, but the prediction about lower rates is offered as a reason for keeping the garage, not as the claim being argued for; (A) is likewise a supporting premise. (E) misreads the planner, who accepts that usage is low and disputes only its cause.

questions.stimulus: Pet columnist: In a survey of dog owners, those who walk their dogs on retractable leashes reported far more incidents of their dogs lunging at passersby than did those who use fixed-length leashes. Evidently, the extra slack that retractable leashes provide encourages dogs to lunge.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the columnist’s argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: relies on reports from dog owners rather than on the judgments of professional trainers
presumes that any dog that lunges at passersby must have been poorly trained
takes for granted that every dog walked on a retractable leash lunges at passersby
overlooks the possibility that owners of dogs prone to lunging are more likely to choose retractable leashes
treats the fact that lunging is undesirable as evidence that it is common
questions.explanation: The columnist infers that the leash causes the lunging from a mere correlation, ignoring that the dogs themselves may differ: owners of excitable, lunge-prone dogs might favor retractable leashes, which is (D). (A) is tempting because self-reports can be unreliable, but nothing in the argument turns on the owners being worse judges than trainers of whether their dogs lunge. (C) attributes a claim about every dog that the columnist never makes.

questions.stimulus: Restaurant owner: Last spring we began printing calorie counts on our menu. Since then, sales of our two highest-calorie desserts have fallen by nearly a third, while sales of our fruit plates have risen. So the calorie counts led many of our customers to choose lighter desserts.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the restaurant owner’s argument?
choices: Over the same period, dessert sales at nearby restaurants that do not print calorie counts showed no comparable shift.
Several customers have told the owner that they appreciate seeing calorie counts on the menu.
The restaurant’s highest-calorie desserts are also among its most expensive desserts.
Many of the restaurant’s customers say they rarely read the menu closely before ordering.
Last spring the restaurant also hired a new pastry chef, who redesigned the fruit plates.
questions.explanation: The owner attributes a sales shift to the calorie counts, so the argument is helped by evidence that the shift did not happen where there were no calorie counts, as (A) shows; that makes a general change in tastes a less likely cause. (B) is tempting but shows only that customers like the counts, not that the counts changed what they ordered. (E) offers a rival explanation and (D) suggests customers ignored the counts, so both weaken.

questions.stimulus: The Ridgeway Observatory replaced its telescope with a new one whose much larger mirror gathers far more light, making faint galaxies easier to detect. Yet in its first year of use, the new telescope detected fewer faint galaxies in total than the old telescope had detected in its last year.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Telescopes with larger mirrors are more expensive to build than those with smaller mirrors.
The old telescope had been in use at the observatory for several decades.
Faint galaxies are considerably harder to detect than bright ones.
The observatory’s astronomers had expected the new telescope to detect many more faint galaxies than the old one.
In its first year, the new telescope was often shut down for calibration and so observed for far fewer hours.
questions.explanation: A better instrument can still produce a smaller total if it is used much less, and (E) says the new telescope spent far less time observing, which resolves the puzzle. (D) merely restates the expectation that makes the result surprising, and (C) is true of both telescopes alike, so it cannot explain a difference between them.

questions.stimulus: At Corwin Insurance, most employees who requested a standing desk last year received one. Of the employees who received standing desks, most reported less back pain at the end of the year than at the start. Among employees who requested a standing desk but did not receive one, reports of back pain were essentially unchanged over the year.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Most Corwin employees reported less back pain at the end of last year than at the start.
Standing desks are the most effective means of reducing back pain among office workers.
Using a standing desk may have helped reduce back pain for some Corwin employees.
Corwin employees who did not request standing desks reported no change in back pain.
Employees who received standing desks used them for most of each workday.
questions.explanation: The comparison between requesters who did and did not get desks gives modest support to the hedged claim in (C) that the desks may have helped some employees. (A) is the tempting trap: the statements concern only employees who requested desks, and nothing indicates that they make up most of the company. (B) is far too strong, and (D) and (E) concern matters the statements never address.

questions.stimulus: Principal: Our school stopped assigning weekend homework this year in order to reduce student stress. Yet students’ average score on the annual stress survey is no lower this year than it was last year. So eliminating weekend homework has not reduced student stress.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the principal’s argument?
choices: Nothing else at the school this year raised student stress enough to mask a reduction caused by the policy.
Students who no longer have weekend homework spend more time on extracurricular activities.
Reducing the amount of homework is the single most effective way for a school to reduce student stress.
Students’ average score on the stress survey was higher this year than it was last year.
Most students had been completing their weekend homework before the policy took effect.
questions.explanation: Unchanged survey scores show the policy failed only if nothing else pushed stress up at the same time; if some other change raised stress by as much as the policy lowered it, the flat scores would hide a real effect. That is (A). (C) is tempting but goes much further than needed: the argument concerns whether this policy worked, not whether homework reduction is the best method. (D) is not required, since unchanged scores are enough for the argument.

questions.stimulus:
Ana: The old mill on Fenwick Creek should be restored and opened as a museum. It is the town’s last surviving link to the industry on which the town was founded, and visitors would learn how our community grew.

Ben: The mill is certainly the most historically important building in town. But restoring it would cost far more than the town could ever raise. A plaque and a small exhibit at the library would preserve the mill’s story at a fraction of the cost.
questions.stem: The dialogue most strongly supports the claim that Ana and Ben agree that
choices: the mill should be restored and opened as a museum
restoring the mill would cost more than the town could raise
a library exhibit is an adequate substitute for a museum
the history associated with the mill is worth preserving in some form
visitors would be more interested in a museum than in a library exhibit
questions.explanation: Ana wants a museum to keep the mill’s history alive, and Ben calls the mill historically important and proposes a cheaper way to preserve its story, so both value preserving that history, as (D) says. (A) is Ana’s view only, while (B) and (C) are Ben’s alone. Neither speaker compares visitor interest, so (E) is unsupported.

questions.stimulus: Marketing director: Customers who bought our Lumo vacuum with the extended warranty brought it in for repairs less often than customers who bought it without the warranty. The warranty includes a free yearly tune-up that other customers do not receive. So the tune-up must be reducing breakdowns.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the marketing director’s argument?
choices: Customers without the extended warranty must pay the full cost of any repair.
During each yearly tune-up, technicians fix any malfunction they find, and such fixes are not recorded as repair visits.
Lumo vacuums break down less often than most competing vacuums do.
Most customers who bought the extended warranty brought their vacuums in for the yearly tune-up.
The extended warranty costs about one-fifth as much as the vacuum itself.
questions.explanation: The director treats fewer recorded repair visits as evidence of fewer breakdowns. (B) shows the comparison is skewed: warranty holders’ malfunctions are often fixed during tune-ups and never counted as repairs, so their lower repair count need not mean fewer breakdowns. (D) strengthens the argument by confirming that warranty holders actually got the tune-ups, and (A), if anything, strengthens it: customers who must pay for repairs would tend to bring vacuums in less often, yet they still had more repair visits.

questions.stimulus: Manager: An employee’s request to work a flexible schedule should be granted whenever the employee’s duties do not require being present at fixed hours, provided that granting the request would not shift any work onto coworkers and the employee has met every deadline during the past six months.
questions.stem: The principle stated above most helps to justify the reasoning in which one of the following arguments?
choices: Rina’s duties do not require fixed hours, and she has met every deadline this year. So her request for a flexible schedule should be granted, even though coworkers would have to cover her morning calls.
Tomas has met every deadline for six months, and his flexible schedule would not burden his coworkers. So his request should be granted, even though he must staff the front desk from nine to five.
Lena’s duties do not require fixed hours, and no work would shift to her coworkers. But she missed a deadline last month, so her request for a flexible schedule should be denied.

Omar’s request would shift no work to his coworkers, and his duties do not require fixed hours. So his request should be granted, since his supervisor considers him one of the department’s best performers.
Priya’s work can be done at any hour, she has not missed a deadline in over a year, and her team confirms that none of her tasks would fall to them. So her request should be granted.
questions.explanation: The principle says a request should be granted when all three conditions hold, and only (E) establishes all three: no fixed hours, no missed deadlines in the past six months, and no work shifted to coworkers. (C) is the attractive trap: Lena fails one condition, but the principle states only when requests should be granted, so it cannot justify denying hers. (A) and (B) each fail a condition outright, and (D) never establishes that Omar has met his deadlines.

questions.stimulus: Council member: Every project paid for from the city’s parks budget must be approved by the neighborhood advisory board, and the board approves only projects that are open to the public. The proposed rooftop garden on City Hall would be reachable only through a secured employee entrance. Thus, the rooftop garden cannot be paid for from the parks budget.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the council member’s argument can be properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: The advisory board has approved every project it has reviewed that is open to the public.
Some projects paid for from the parks budget are not open to the public.
No facility that is reachable only through a secured employee entrance is open to the public.
The rooftop garden would benefit city employees more than it would benefit other residents.
If a project is open to the public, it can be paid for from the parks budget.
questions.explanation: The chain is: parks funding requires board approval, and board approval requires being open to the public. The missing link connects “reachable only through a secured employee entrance” to “not open to the public,” and (C) supplies it, so the garden cannot get approval and therefore cannot get funding. (A) and (E) reverse the conditionals and say what is enough for approval or funding, which cannot show that the garden is barred. (B) conflicts with the stated rules.

questions.stimulus: Science writer: Ten years ago, amateur astronomers discovered about 30 percent of all newly identified asteroids; last year, they discovered under 5 percent. Clearly, amateurs are finding fewer asteroids than they once did, perhaps because light pollution has worsened in the suburbs where many of them live.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the science writer’s argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: relies on figures drawn from only two years
overlooks the possibility that the total number of asteroids discovered each year has risen sharply
presumes without justification that light pollution affects professional astronomers less than it affects amateurs
takes for granted that most amateur astronomers live in suburbs
confuses a decline in amateurs’ interest in asteroids with a decline in their skill
questions.explanation: A falling share of discoveries does not show a falling number: if total discoveries grew enough, for example because professional survey telescopes came online, amateurs could be finding as many asteroids as before or more. (B) identifies this. (A) is tempting, but the argument’s problem is not too few data points; even many years of shrinking percentages would leave the same gap. (D) misstates the writer, who says only that “many” amateurs live in suburbs, and the light-pollution remark is offered only as a possible explanation.

questions.stimulus: At the Linden animal shelter, cats housed in the shelter’s quiet rooms have long been adopted more quickly than cats housed in the noisy main kennel area. Last fall, the shelter soundproofed another room and moved half of its main-area cats into it. Yet the cats that were moved were not adopted any more quickly than before.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why moving the cats did not shorten their adoption times?
choices: Cats in the main kennel area are frequently exposed to the noise of barking dogs.
Most people who adopt cats from the shelter visit on weekends.
The newly soundproofed room is larger than the shelter’s other quiet rooms.
Some cats in the main kennel area have been adopted within a day of arriving.
Until last fall, the shelter placed only its calmest and most sociable cats in quiet rooms.
questions.explanation: If the shelter had been putting its calmest, most sociable cats in the quiet rooms, those cats’ faster adoptions reflected their temperaments rather than the quiet, so giving other cats a quiet room would not be expected to help. That is (E). (A) is tempting because it explains why the main area might seem unappealing, but it gives no reason why removing the noise failed to help. (C) would, if anything, lead one to expect better results.

questions.stimulus: Food critic: A restaurant’s reputation for freshness depends on its use of ingredients that are in season. But a restaurant that builds its menu entirely around seasonal ingredients must change that menu several times a year, and frequent menu changes make it hard for a kitchen to prepare dishes consistently. Moreover, diners seldom return to a restaurant whose dishes are inconsistent. Thus, ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: a restaurant that builds its menu entirely around seasonal ingredients risks losing repeat customers
no restaurant can have both a reputation for freshness and a loyal base of repeat customers
restaurants that want repeat customers should avoid using seasonal ingredients
a reputation for freshness is less valuable to a restaurant than consistency is
restaurants whose dishes are consistent seldom use seasonal ingredients
questions.explanation: The premises connect an all-seasonal menu to frequent changes, frequent changes to difficulty with consistency, and inconsistency to diners not returning, so the cautious conclusion in (A) follows. (B) is the attractive overreach: the critic says only that consistency is hard, not impossible, and a restaurant could use seasonal ingredients without building its whole menu around them. (C) and (D) add recommendations or rankings the premises do not support, and (E) reverses the direction of the reasoning.

questions.stimulus: Historian: Most of the buildings on Market Street date from before 1900, and most buildings in the city that date from before 1900 have been designated as landmarks. So most of the buildings on Market Street have been designated as landmarks.
questions.stem: The pattern of questionable reasoning in the argument above is most similar to that in which one of the following?
choices: Most members of the choir are sopranos, and most of the choir’s sopranos also play an instrument. So some members of the choir play an instrument.
Most of the library’s patrons are students, and all students receive free borrowing privileges. So most of the library’s patrons receive free borrowing privileges.
No member of the hiking club smokes, and most members of the hiking club are runners. So most runners do not smoke.
Most of the paintings in the east gallery are oil paintings, and most of the museum’s oil paintings are on loan. So most of the paintings in the east gallery are on loan.
Most of the apples grown on the Garza farm are sold at market. So most of the produce grown on the Garza farm is sold at market.
questions.explanation: The historian chains two “most” statements as if they guaranteed overlap: the Market Street buildings could fall mostly among the pre-1900 buildings that are not landmarks. (D) makes exactly that move with paintings, oil paintings, and loans. (A) is the strongest trap because it shares the “most… most” form, but its conclusion is only “some,” which does validly follow; (B) is also valid because its second premise says “all.” (C) and (E) are flawed, but in different ways, by reversing a relationship and by moving from a part to the whole.

questions.stimulus: Consumer advocate: Brightline advertises that its LED bulbs last 20 years, a figure based on tests of bulbs in open fixtures at room temperature. But heat shortens the life of LED bulbs, and most household light fixtures are enclosed, trapping heat around the bulb. So in most households, Brightline bulbs will last well short of 20 years.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the consumer advocate’s argument depends?
choices: Brightline’s competitors base their lifespan claims on more realistic tests.
Trapped heat in enclosed fixtures is the main cause of LED bulb failure in households.
Brightline bulbs are not designed in a way that protects them from the effects of heat in enclosed fixtures.
Bulbs in enclosed fixtures fail sooner than bulbs in any other kind of fixture.
Brightline knowingly exaggerated the expected lifespan of its bulbs.
questions.explanation: The advocate moves from a general fact, that heat shortens LED life, to a prediction about Brightline bulbs in particular. If Brightline bulbs were built to withstand the heat of enclosed fixtures, that prediction would fail, so the argument requires (C). (B) is tempting but too strong: heat need only shorten these bulbs’ lives significantly, not be the leading cause of failure. (D) and (E) are likewise stronger than anything the argument needs.

questions.stimulus: Superintendent: Critics claim that moving our high school’s start time from 7:30 to 8:30 has hurt attendance at after-school sports, because practices now end after dark. But this complaint is unfounded. The number of students on our sports teams this year is actually slightly higher than it was last year.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most undermines the superintendent’s defense?
choices: Attendance at the school’s evening theater and music rehearsals has also declined since the start time changed.
Unlike in previous years, students this year may remain on a team’s roster without attending a minimum number of practices.
Practices at neighboring schools that kept a 7:30 start time also end after dark during part of the year.
Membership on the school’s sports teams rose more this year than in any of the previous five years.
Several parents have complained that the later start time conflicts with their work schedules.
questions.explanation: The critics’ complaint is about attendance at practices, but the superintendent answers with roster size. (B) shows why that answer misses: with attendance no longer required to stay on a roster, rosters can grow even while practice attendance falls. (A) is the attractive trap, since it fits the critics’ general worry, but it concerns different activities and leaves the superintendent’s evidence about sports untouched. (D) supports the defense, and (C) and (E) do not bear on whether sports attendance fell.

questions.stimulus: Pelham city ordinance: A food truck may operate downtown only if it holds a downtown permit. A downtown permit is issued only to trucks that have passed the city’s fire inspection. A truck that uses a propane grill passes the fire inspection only if the grill has an automatic shutoff valve.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Any food truck that has passed the city’s fire inspection may operate downtown.
Every food truck whose propane grill has an automatic shutoff valve passes the fire inspection.
A food truck that does not use a propane grill can be issued a downtown permit if it applies for one.
Some food trucks that operate downtown use propane grills.
A truck that has only ever used a propane grill lacking an automatic shutoff valve cannot be issued a downtown permit.
questions.explanation: A permit requires passing inspection, and a truck with a propane grill passes only if the grill has a shutoff valve; a truck whose propane grill has never had one could never have passed, so it cannot get a permit, as (E) says. (A) and (B) treat necessary conditions as if they were sufficient, (C) assumes that lacking a propane grill guarantees a permit, and (D) asserts the existence of trucks that the rules never mention.

questions.stimulus: Animal behaviorist: Parrots that pluck out their own feathers are commonly assumed to be bored. But feather plucking often begins in parrots that already have plenty of toys and companionship, and it frequently stops after a change in the bird’s diet. This suggests that, in many cases, plucking has a nutritional rather than a psychological cause. Owners of parrots that pluck should therefore consult an avian veterinarian before buying more toys.
questions.stem: The claim that in many cases plucking has a nutritional rather than a psychological cause plays which one of the following roles in the animal behaviorist’s argument?
choices: It is a conclusion drawn from evidence in the argument and is offered in support of the argument’s main conclusion.
It is the main conclusion of the argument.
It is a view that the argument is designed to call into question.
It is a premise offered in support of the view that plucking is usually caused by boredom.
It is a hypothesis offered to explain why parrot owners tend to buy more toys.
questions.explanation: The claim is drawn from the observations about toys and diet (“This suggests that”), and it in turn supports the recommendation introduced by “therefore,” so it is an intermediate conclusion, as (A) says. (B) is the trap: the argument’s final point is the advice to owners, which the nutritional claim supports. (C) describes the boredom assumption, not this claim, and (D) has the claim supporting the very view it opposes.

questions.stimulus: Office manager: Only employees who have registered a vehicle with security may receive a parking pass, and security registers a vehicle only for an employee who has completed the safety orientation. Thus, Dana, who works only on weekends, will not receive a parking pass.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the office manager’s argument can be properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Every employee who has completed the safety orientation will receive a parking pass.
The safety orientation is held only on weekdays.
Most employees who work only on weekends have not completed the safety orientation.
No employee who works only on weekends has completed the safety orientation.
Employees who work only on weekends rarely drive to work.
questions.explanation: A pass requires a registered vehicle, and registration requires completing the orientation. If no weekend-only employee has completed it, as (D) states, Dana cannot have a registered vehicle and so cannot receive a pass. (B) is the tempting choice, but an orientation held on weekdays could still have been attended by Dana, perhaps before she switched to weekends, so it does not guarantee the conclusion. (C) says only “most,” which leaves open that Dana completed it, and (A) reverses the conditional.

questions.stimulus: Local historian: The diary of Hester Vane, who lived in Millbrook in the 1840s, describes crossing a covered bridge over the Tull River. Yet no other surviving record from that decade mentions such a bridge in Millbrook, and the town’s earliest map, drawn in 1852, shows no bridge over the Tull. So the bridge Vane described must have been in some other town along the river.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions most helps in evaluating the local historian’s argument?
choices: Is Vane’s diary the oldest surviving document written by a Millbrook resident?
Were covered bridges more expensive to build in the 1840s than uncovered bridges?
Did some event destroy structures along the Tull River in Millbrook between the 1840s and 1852?
How long did Vane continue to live in Millbrook after the 1840s?
Were most residents of Millbrook in the 1840s able to read and write?
questions.explanation: The historian relies on the bridge’s absence from later evidence, especially the 1852 map. If a flood or similar event had destroyed a bridge in Millbrook before 1852, the map’s silence would be expected even though the bridge had existed, so the answer to (C) bears directly on the argument. (A) sounds important, but whether the diary is the oldest document does not affect whether the bridge was in Millbrook. The other questions do not bear on where the bridge stood.

questions.stimulus: Restaurant reviewer: Café Morrow’s menu used to state that its bread was baked in-house. When the café began buying its bread from a local bakery, it simply removed that statement. Some diners complain that the café should have announced the change. But the café never made a false claim; it merely stopped making a true claim once the claim became false. So the café did nothing wrong.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, would most help to justify the restaurant reviewer’s argument?
choices: Diners are entitled to be told the source of every ingredient in the food a restaurant serves them.
A business does nothing wrong in changing its suppliers so long as the quality of its products is unaffected.
A business that has made a false claim about its products should correct that claim promptly and publicly.
Whether a business has wronged its customers depends entirely on whether any of those customers was actually harmed.
A business that withdraws a claim about its products as soon as the claim becomes false need not announce the withdrawal.
questions.explanation: The reviewer’s defense is that the café stopped making the in-house claim at the moment it became false and so owed diners no announcement; (E) states exactly that principle. (B) is the strongest trap, but the reviewer says nothing about bread quality, and the diners’ complaint concerns the lack of an announcement, not the change of supplier. (C) is on topic but applies only to false claims, which the café never made, and (D) depends on harm, which the argument never discusses.

questions.stimulus: Councilor Reyes: Supporters of the proposed bus-only lane on Garnet Avenue claim that it will cut commute times for bus riders, because a similar lane in Easton did so. But buses in Easton run twice as often as ours do, so Easton’s results tell us little about what would happen on Garnet Avenue. Hence, the bus lane will not cut commute times for our riders.
questions.stem: The argument’s reasoning is questionable in that the argument
choices: relies on an analogy between two cities that differ in a relevant respect
takes the inadequacy of the evidence offered for a claim as showing that the claim is false
attacks the motives of the lane’s supporters rather than the reasoning they offer
presumes that bus frequency is the only factor that affects bus riders’ commute times
overlooks the possibility that the bus lane would benefit people who drive private cars
questions.explanation: Reyes legitimately shows that the Easton comparison is weak support, but then concludes that the lane will not cut commute times; a poorly supported claim may still be true, so (B) names the flaw. (A) is the main trap: the weak analogy belongs to the supporters, and pointing it out is the sound part of Reyes’s reasoning. (D) also tempts, but Reyes treats frequency only as one relevant difference, not as the sole factor, and (E) concerns drivers rather than bus riders.

questions.stimulus: Veterinary researcher: Dogs fed from puzzle feeders, which make a dog work to get its food out, show fewer destructive behaviors at home than dogs fed from ordinary bowls. This suggests that the mental effort of working out food reduces the boredom that drives much destructive behavior in dogs.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the veterinary researcher’s argument?
choices: Dogs switched from bowls to puzzle feeders showed fewer destructive behaviors over the following weeks.
Owners who buy puzzle feeders tend to spend more time exercising their dogs than other owners do.
Puzzle feeders slow down dogs’ eating, which can reduce some digestive problems.
Some dogs fed from puzzle feeders still chew furniture when left alone.
Destructive behavior is more common among some breeds of dogs than among others.
questions.explanation: The original evidence compares different dogs, so the difference might reflect the owners or the dogs rather than the feeders. (A) shows the same dogs improving after the switch, which makes the feeder a more likely cause. (B) offers a competing explanation and so weakens; (C) is tempting because it describes another effect of the feeders, but digestion has nothing to do with boredom-driven behavior.

questions.stimulus: Astronomy club president: Some members want us to double the number of public stargazing nights, since attendance has been strong. But the program depends entirely on a handful of volunteers who bring and operate their own telescopes, and several of them say they are already stretched thin. Expanding in a way that drives those volunteers away would end the program altogether. So we should not double the number of nights.
questions.stem: The principle underlying the argument above is most similar to the principle underlying which one of the following arguments?
choices: Restaurant owner: Our lunch special is very popular, but we lose money on every one we serve. So we should raise its price, even if fewer customers order it.
School principal: Some parents want us to add field trips. But each trip uses money that would otherwise go to new books, and our book budget is already tight. So we should not add field trips.
Library director: Our volunteer tutors tell us they greatly enjoy their work. So we can extend tutoring hours without hiring any paid staff.

Garden coordinator: Neighbors want us to add a second garden plot. But our garden depends on a few retirees who already feel overworked, and if they quit there would be no garden at all. So we should not add the plot.
Mayor: The farmers market has become very crowded. It should move to a larger lot, even though vendors there would pay higher fees, because more customers would benefit the vendors as well.
questions.explanation: The president’s principle is that an activity should not be expanded if expanding it would likely drive off the few people it depends on and so end it entirely. (D) applies the same principle to a garden kept up by overworked retirees. (B) is the closest trap, but it rests on a budget tradeoff between two goods, not on losing the people who make the activity possible; (C) shares the volunteer theme but reaches the opposite kind of conclusion from a different consideration.

questions.stimulus: Office supply retailer: Of the customers who bought our Tallis desk chair last year, most also bought the optional lumbar cushion. Of the customers who returned the chair, most had not bought the cushion. No customer bought more than one chair.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Most customers who did not buy the lumbar cushion returned the chair.
Buying the lumbar cushion made customers less likely to return the chair.
The return rate was higher among customers who skipped the cushion than among those who bought it.
More chairs were returned by customers who bought the lumbar cushion than by customers who did not buy it.
Most customers who bought the Tallis chair last year kept it.
questions.explanation: Customers without the cushion were the smaller group, yet they accounted for more of the returns, so their return rate must have been higher, which is (C). (B) is the most tempting choice, but the data show only a correlation; customers who skipped the cushion may differ in other ways, such as being less committed to the chair. (A) and (E) need information about the overall return rate, which is not given, and (D) contradicts the second statement.

passages.title: Court-Appointed Expert Witnesses
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
Passage A

In most common-law jurisdictions a trial judge may, on a party’s motion or on the judge’s own initiative, appoint an expert witness of the court’s choosing. The power is seldom used, and its advocates attribute this to judicial timidity. There are, however, sound reasons for the reluctance.

First, an expert introduced to the jury as the court’s own arrives cloaked in a neutrality that no party’s expert can match. Jurors told that one witness was chosen by the judge are apt to treat that witness’s opinion not as evidence to be weighed but as a verdict to be ratified, so that a single person who was never meant to decide the case effectively does so.

Second, the appointment itself is far from neutral. In fields where the science is unsettled—the reliability of certain forensic techniques, say, or the causes of a rare illness—competent specialists disagree, and to select one of them is to select a side. A judge, who by hypothesis lacks the expertise to resolve the dispute, is poorly placed to recognize that a choice of person is also a choice of doctrine, and the jury will never learn that such a choice was made at all.

Third, the court’s expert is shielded from the testing that adversarial procedure supplies. A lawyer who sharply cross-examines the judge’s own witness risks appearing to quarrel with the judge, and few lawyers will run that risk. The remedy for partisan expertise is not to abandon the adversarial method but to strengthen it: earlier disclosure of expert reports, and pretrial hearings at which opposing experts must confront each other’s reasoning.

Passage B

Litigants do not hire experts at random. They interview several and retain the one whose views best serve their case—or whose views, for an adequate fee, can be made to serve it. The result in a technical dispute is often two confident witnesses whose conclusions are irreconcilable, presented to jurors who have no basis for choosing between them. Research with mock jurors suggests that in such contests jurors tend to credit the expert who seems more poised and likable, a standard bearing little relation to the merits.

A court-appointed expert addresses this problem not by replacing the parties’ experts but by giving jurors a fixed point against which to measure them. The parties remain free to call their own witnesses and to cross-examine the court’s. And if jurors give the court’s expert more weight than either party’s, that is hardly a defect: an expert chosen for competence rather than for persuasiveness deserves more weight.

Nor need the selection be left to a judge’s unaided guesswork. Courts can ask each side to nominate candidates and appoint someone acceptable to both, or can request that a professional body propose a panel from which the judge chooses. Where a field is genuinely divided, the appointed expert can be instructed to report the range of respectable opinion rather than only her own. And the judge should tell jurors plainly that the court’s expert is a witness like any other, whose testimony they are free to accept or reject.

passages.title: Serial Publication and the Victorian Novel
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
When Charles Dickens’s The Pickwick Papers began appearing in monthly parts in 1836, it helped establish a mode of publication that dominated British fiction for decades: novels issued in installments, as separate numbers or in magazines, over a year or more. The literary historian Ines Varga has argued that many of the features for which Victorian novels were long criticized are best understood as products of this mode. The suspenseful endings of installments, the proliferation of subplots, and the habit of tagging minor characters with a signature phrase or mannerism are, on Varga’s account, not lapses of craft but rational responses to what she calls “serial form.” She has little patience for earlier critics who dismissed such features as “padding paid for by the page,” a judgment she describes as mistaking the conditions of an art for its failures.

Varga’s account is persuasive in outline, but it fails to clarify what serial form is supposed to have demanded. In her usage the term does double duty. Sometimes it refers to the situation of readers, who met a novel in fragments weeks apart and so needed reminders of who was who and reasons to buy the next number. At other times it refers to the situation of writers, many of whom composed each installment shortly before it was due, could not revise chapters already in print, and learned of the public’s response while the story was still unfinished. These are distinct pressures, and they predict different things: the first should leave its mark wherever readers encountered a text intermittently, however it was written; the second, wherever a text was written under deadline, however it was read.

Varga’s evidence, moreover, rests on a comparison whose significance she does not establish. She shows that the features in question are markedly more common in serialized novels than in novels first issued complete, typically in three volumes for the circulating libraries. But the comparison is telling only if the two groups of novels are otherwise alike, and Varga simply assumes that they are. If publishers offered serialization chiefly to established popular authors, whose habits of plotting predated their first serials, or to comic and sensational stories, in which suspense and broadly drawn minor characters were long-standing conventions, the difference she documents may owe less to the mode of publication than to the authors and stories it attracted.

The case of the novelist Edmund Carrow complicates matters further. Carrow, unusually, finished each of his novels before its first installment appeared, yet his books abound in cliffhangers and in minor characters identified by recurring tics. Varga treats Carrow as confirming her thesis, since he wrote knowing that readers would meet his work in parts. Perhaps so—but his novels contain almost none of the abandoned subplots and inconsistencies of detail that she also attributes to serial form. Carrow thus suggests that the two pressures her term conflates operated independently. Varga has identified a real cause; what her account needs is a finer description of how that cause worked.

passages.title: Unbalanced accounts in the Orlen Valley ledgers
passages.text:
When the household account books kept by farming families in the Orlen Valley between roughly 1780 and 1860 were first catalogued in the 1950s, archivists noticed a curious feature. Entries recording loans of grain, labor, and tools between neighboring households almost never balance. When such a debt was repaid, the repayment was nearly always a little more or a little less than the original loan, and the difference was carried forward rather than settled. Early commentators took this as evidence of careless bookkeeping, or of a rural population that lacked the arithmetic to reconcile its accounts.

The anthropologist Teodora Halvik has offered a different explanation. In her view, the imbalances were deliberate. Among Orlen households, she argues, an exchange that ended with nothing owed on either side ended the relationship as well; to repay a neighbor exactly was to announce that one no longer wished to be bound to that neighbor. Keeping a small remainder perpetually outstanding was thus a way of keeping the relationship open. Halvik notes that the ledgers have a local expression for such an account: it is said to be “on the long thread.”

Halvik’s evidence is of several kinds. The same households that left their neighbors’ accounts unbalanced kept precise records of their dealings with grain merchants from outside the valley, and those accounts were closed to the last measure whenever a transaction was complete. Nor were the remainders random: they were small, typically less than a tenth of the original loan, and the direction of the imbalance tended to alternate, so that each household was in turn creditor and debtor. Finally, in the few cases in which an account between neighbors was closed exactly, parish records from the same months frequently note a dispute between the two families, a lawsuit, or the departure of one of them from the valley.

The ledger of the Brenn household illustrates the mechanism. In the spring of 1812 the Brenns lent eight bushels of rye to the neighboring Tamm family. At harvest the Tamms returned nine, leaving the Brenns owing the Tamms one bushel. That winter the Brenns repaid the bushel with two days of labor on the Tamms’ threshing floor—work the ledger values at slightly more than a bushel, so that the Tamms now owed the Brenns a small fraction. The account continued in this way, alternating, for thirty-one years. It was closed only in 1843, the year in which the parish register records that a quarrel over a boundary stone had divided the two families.

If Halvik is right, the ledgers are not failed attempts at reckoning but successful records of a different kind: they tracked not merely what was owed but who remained bound to whom. Orlen arithmetic, on this account, was exact where exactness served a purpose and deliberately loose where looseness did.

passages.title: Recruitment failure in the slate pearlmussel
passages.text:
For most of the twentieth century, the slate pearlmussel was among the most abundant freshwater mussels in the Halder River. By the 1970s, however, surveys upstream of the Ostrow Dam, completed in 1931, were finding fewer of the mussels each decade, and the decline was attributed to the industrial pollution and agricultural sediment that had degraded much of the river. A regional cleanup program begun in 1978 cut discharges sharply, and by the late 1980s water quality above the dam met every standard the program had set. The mussels continued to decline.

In 1994 the biologist Renata Kovač proposed that the problem lay not in the water but in the mussel’s life cycle. Like many freshwater mussels, the slate pearlmussel cannot complete its development on its own. A female releases larvae, called glochidia, that must clamp onto the gills of a fish, where they become encapsulated in its tissue and live as parasites for several weeks before dropping off as juvenile mussels. Kovač found that glochidia exposed in the laboratory to a dozen fish species transformed successfully only on the Halder herring, a migratory fish that once ascended the river each spring to spawn; on other species they were shed within days. The dam, which had no fish passage, had ended the herring’s runs. Kovač then aged living mussels by counting the annual growth rings on their shells. Downstream of the dam, mussels of every age were present; upstream, nearly all were more than sixty years old—older, that is, than the dam itself. Because adults can live for most of a century, she argued, the upstream population had been reproductively dead for decades while appearing merely diminished.

Kovač urged that funds be redirected from further water-quality measures to fish passage at the dam, and her proposal met resistance. Some biologists objected that laboratory results might not reflect conditions in the river, where glochidia might use hosts that fare poorly in tanks. Others noted that the dam had also caused fine sediment to accumulate above it, and that juvenile mussels, which burrow and feed in the riverbed, are more sensitive to such sediment than adults are. The missing age classes, these critics argued, might reflect where juveniles could survive rather than whether they were being produced.

A fish lift began operating at the dam in 2008. Within two years, herring caught upstream were found carrying encysted glochidia, and surveys in 2015 recovered juvenile pearlmussels above the dam for the first time in living memory—including in reaches where sediment had not measurably changed. Recruitment was nonetheless markedly lower in the siltiest reaches, suggesting that Kovač’s critics had identified a real, though secondary, constraint. The episode is now often cited as a caution: a population of long-lived adults can conceal a failure of reproduction for generations.
