questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately characterizes the relationship between the two passages?
choices: Passage A describes the historical development of a procedural power, while passage B evaluates several proposals for reforming that power.
Passage A and passage B both criticize a procedural power, but they propose different remedies for the defects each identifies in it.
Passage A argues that a procedural power should be used more often, while passage B argues that it should be reserved for unusually technical disputes.
Passage A argues against the use of a procedural power, while passage B argues for its use and proposes measures that bear on some problems passage A raises.
Passage A identifies problems with a procedural power, while passage B argues that those problems are less serious than the problems with every alternative to it.
questions.explanation: Passage A gives three reasons for judges' reluctance to appoint their own experts and recommends strengthening adversarial testing instead; passage B defends court-appointed experts and offers safeguards (joint nomination, professional panels, a range-of-opinion report, a jury instruction) that answer A's worries about selection and deference, so D is correct. E is the most tempting trap: B argues that dueling party experts are a serious problem, but it never surveys 'every alternative' and never considers A's proposed reform. B misreads passage B as critical, and C reverses passage A's stance.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is mentioned in passage A but not in passage B?
choices: the possibility that a judge could ask a professional body to propose candidates for appointment
the reluctance of attorneys to cross-examine forcefully a witness whom the judge has chosen
the existence of technical fields in which competent specialists disagree with one another
the tendency of jurors to credit whichever of two experts seems more poised and likable
the right of parties to present their own experts even when the court has appointed one
questions.explanation: The third paragraph of passage A says a lawyer who sharply cross-examines the judge's witness 'risks appearing to quarrel with the judge'; passage B says only that parties 'remain free' to cross-examine the court's expert, which is a point about permission, not reluctance, so B is correct. C is the likeliest trap, but it appears in both passages (A's 'competent specialists disagree'; B's 'Where a field is genuinely divided'). A, D, and E appear only in passage B.

questions.stem: The author of passage B suggests that some experts retained by litigants are too
choices: accommodating
cautious
specialized
numerous
inexpensive
questions.explanation: The first paragraph of passage B says litigants retain the expert whose views 'for an adequate fee, can be made to serve' their case, implying that some experts are too willing to fit their views to the party paying them: too accommodating (A). E inverts the reference to fees, which concerns experts' willingness to be paid for favorable views, not their cost; B, C, and D have no support in the passage.

questions.stem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree over whether
choices: jurors are likely to give the testimony of a court-appointed expert more weight than the testimony of a party’s expert
parties should be permitted to cross-examine an expert whom the court has appointed
competent specialists sometimes reach conflicting conclusions on technical questions
the testimony of experts retained by litigants tends to reflect the interests of those litigants
the weight jurors are likely to give a court-appointed expert’s testimony is a reason against appointing such experts
questions.explanation: Passage A's first objection is that jurors will treat the court's expert's opinion 'as a verdict to be ratified'; passage B replies that if jurors give that expert more weight, 'that is hardly a defect,' since an expert chosen for competence deserves it. They thus disagree about whether such deference counts against appointment (E). A is the strong trap: passage B does not deny that jurors will give the court's expert more weight (its 'if' clause concedes the possibility), so the disagreement is about the significance of that weight, not its existence. C and D are points both authors accept, and B is something passage A never addresses.

questions.stem: The relationship between passage A and passage B is most analogous to the relationship between the documents described in which one of the following?
choices: an essay titled “Why Arbitrators Should Rely on the Parties’ Rival Appraisals” and an essay titled “Improving the Exchange of Appraisal Reports Before Arbitration Hearings”
an essay titled “In Defense of Arbitrator-Commissioned Appraisals” and an essay titled “The Dangers of Letting Arbitrators Choose Their Own Appraisers”
an essay titled “The Hidden Hazards of Arbitrator-Commissioned Appraisals” and an essay titled “A Benchmark Between Rival Valuations: The Case for Arbitrator-Commissioned Appraisals”
an essay titled “The Hidden Hazards of Arbitrator-Commissioned Appraisals” and an essay titled “How Parties to Arbitration Can Choose Better Appraisers of Their Own”
an essay titled “A Short History of Appraisal in Commercial Arbitration” and an essay titled “A Benchmark Between Rival Valuations: The Case for Arbitrator-Commissioned Appraisals”
questions.explanation: Passage A criticizes a decision maker's appointing its own supposedly neutral expert, and passage B defends that practice as giving decision makers a fixed point between rival partisan experts; C reproduces both stances and B's 'fixed point' rationale. B reverses the order of the two stances. D is the closest trap: its first title matches passage A, but its second is about improving the parties' own experts, which is closer to passage A's remedy than to passage B's defense. A has two essays favoring the adversarial approach, and E's first essay is historical rather than critical.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is a criticism that the author of passage A would be likely to offer regarding the suggestion in passage B that judges tell jurors the court’s expert is a witness like any other?
choices: Jurors who know that the judge selected the expert are likely to go on treating that expert’s opinion as authoritative regardless of what they are told.
Such an instruction would discourage jurors from giving the court’s expert the additional weight that the expert’s neutrality warrants.
Such an instruction would reveal to jurors a fact about how the expert was selected that they would otherwise never learn.
Such an instruction would make attorneys more willing to cross-examine the court’s expert aggressively, needlessly prolonging trials.
Such an instruction would be unnecessary, since jurors already regard the court’s expert as no more reliable than other witnesses.
questions.explanation: Passage A's first objection is that jurors told a witness was chosen by the judge treat that witness's opinion 'not as evidence to be weighed but as a verdict to be ratified'; an instruction that leaves jurors knowing who chose the expert would not dispel that aura, so A is correct. B states passage B's view of the expert's added weight, not passage A's. C is tempting because passage A says the jury 'will never learn' something, but that refers to the choice of doctrine, and passage A assumes jurors are told who chose the witness. D and E conflict with passage A's own concerns.

questions.stem: The author of passage B would be most likely to regard the remedy proposed in the last sentence of passage A as inadequate on the grounds that it
choices: would deprive the parties of the opportunity to cross-examine opposing experts in the presence of the jury
would leave jurors without an independent reference point for assessing the conflicting conclusions of the parties’ experts
presupposes that judges can choose qualified experts competently without the assistance of the parties
would make litigants’ selection of experts whose views serve their case even more strategic than it already is
would require jurors to master the technical reasoning that the opposing experts present at pretrial hearings
questions.explanation: Passage B locates the problem in jurors having 'no basis for choosing between' two partisan experts, and it presents the court's expert as 'a fixed point against which to measure them'; passage A's remedy (earlier disclosure and pretrial confrontation between the parties' experts) still leaves only partisan experts, so B is correct. C is the most tempting trap because it echoes passage B's phrase 'unaided guesswork,' but passage A's remedy involves no judicial selection of experts at all. E misplaces the jury at pretrial hearings, and A and D have no basis in either passage.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Varga has shown that features of Victorian novels that earlier critics dismissed as flaws of craft were in fact rational responses to the demands of serial publication.
Varga’s account of the influence of serial publication on the Victorian novel is undermined by the case of a novelist who completed his books before serializing them.
Although Varga is right that serial publication shaped the Victorian novel, her account conflates distinct pressures and rests on a comparison of uncertain significance.
The features of Victorian serialized novels are better explained by the pressures that serial publication placed on writers than by those it placed on readers.
Varga’s comparison of serialized novels with novels first issued complete overlooks differences between the kinds of authors and stories in the two groups.
questions.explanation: The author calls Varga's account 'persuasive in outline' and concludes that she 'has identified a real cause,' while the second and fourth paragraphs show that her term conflates two pressures and the third questions her comparison, so C is correct. A states Varga's view without the author's reservations. B overstates the author's attitude toward the Carrow case, which complicates rather than refutes her thesis. D picks one pressure over the other, whereas the author says both operated. E is a single point from the third paragraph.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that Varga’s attitude toward the judgment of earlier critics that certain features of Victorian novels were “padding paid for by the page” can best be described as one of
choices: indifference
sympathy
ambivalence
deference
disapproval
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says Varga 'has little patience' for those critics and describes their judgment as 'mistaking the conditions of an art for its failures,' which is disapproval (E). C is the likeliest trap for readers who notice that the author has reservations about Varga, but those reservations are the author's, not Varga's, and Varga herself is not described as torn about the critics' judgment. A, B, and D are contradicted by her impatience with them.

questions.stem: In using the phrase “does double duty” (second sentence of the second paragraph), the author most probably means that Varga’s term “serial form”
choices: serves both to explain certain features of Victorian novels and to defend those features against earlier critics
covers both publication in separate numbers and publication in magazines
is used both by Varga and by the earlier critics whose judgments about the novels she rejects
is applied, without distinction, to two different sets of circumstances that might have shaped the novels
names both the characteristic features of serialized novels and the conditions that produced those features
questions.explanation: The sentences that follow explain the phrase: 'sometimes' the term refers to readers' situation and 'at other times' to writers', and the author calls these 'distinct pressures,' so D is correct. A is the strongest trap because Varga's account does both explain and defend the features, but the second paragraph is about what the term refers to, not about the uses of her account. B draws on the two formats mentioned in the first paragraph, which the author never says the term blurs. C and E have no support.

questions.stem: The primary function of the third paragraph is to
choices: distinguish two senses of a term that is used in the first paragraph
identify an assumption relied upon by the evidence offered for the view described in the first paragraph
present a case that the view described in the first paragraph is unable to accommodate
explain why the critics mentioned in the first paragraph regarded certain features of novels as flaws
offer evidence that conclusively refutes the view described in the first paragraph
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says Varga's comparison of serialized novels with novels first issued complete 'is telling only if the two groups of novels are otherwise alike, and Varga simply assumes that they are,' and then shows how the groups might differ, so B is correct. A describes the second paragraph and C the fourth (and even the Carrow case is presented as a complication, not as something Varga cannot accommodate). E is too strong: the paragraph raises possibilities introduced by 'if' and says the difference 'may' have another source.

questions.stem: The author mentions “comic and sensational stories” (last sentence of the third paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: indicate one way in which serialized novels might have differed from novels first issued complete other than in their mode of publication
identify the kinds of fiction for which publishers first adopted the practice of issuing novels in installments
suggest that the earlier critics’ dismissal of certain features as padding was justified for some kinds of fiction
illustrate the pressures that serial publication placed on readers who encountered novels in fragments
show that suspenseful endings were more common in novels issued complete than in serialized novels
questions.explanation: The reference appears in an 'if' clause describing ways the two groups of novels Varga compares might not be 'otherwise alike': if serialization went chiefly to genres in which suspense and broadly drawn characters were already conventions, the difference she documents could reflect genre rather than publication mode. That is A. D is tempting because suspense and memorable minor characters relate to readers' needs, but the point here concerns the composition of the comparison groups. B attributes a historical claim the passage never makes, and C and E are unsupported.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that Varga’s interpretation of Carrow’s novels commits her to which one of the following views?
choices: Carrow’s novels contain the abandoned subplots and inconsistencies of detail typical of serialized fiction.
The pressures that serial publication placed on readers and on writers operated independently of each other.
The term “serial form” should be used to refer only to the situation of readers who met novels in installments.
Some of the features she attributes to serial form can arise in a novel whose author did not compose it under installment deadlines.
Novelists who completed their work before serialization were more skilled at plotting than those who wrote installment by installment.
questions.explanation: Carrow finished each novel before serialization, so he did not write under installment deadlines, yet Varga treats his cliffhangers and recurring tics as confirming her thesis; she must therefore hold that features she attributes to serial form can arise without deadline composition (D). B is the most tempting trap, but it is the author's conclusion from the Carrow case, not something Varga's reading requires; the passage says her term 'conflates' the two pressures. C is too strong, since accepting reader-side effects in Carrow does not commit her to dropping the writer-side sense of the term. A is contradicted by the fourth paragraph.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if discovered, would provide the strongest evidence that the conditions under which serial novelists wrote, independently of the conditions under which their readers read, produced some of the features Varga attributes to serial form?
choices: A novelist who completed each of her novels before serialization nonetheless ended nearly every installment with a suspenseful scene.
Novels written month by month for serial publication contain more cliffhangers, subplots, and recurring tics than do novels first issued complete.

A novel delivered to its publisher chapter by chapter against monthly deadlines, but always intended to be issued only in complete form, contains many abandoned subplots and inconsistencies of detail.
Readers of serialized novels often wrote to the authors complaining that they had forgotten who the minor characters were between installments.
A novel composed slowly over several years and first issued in complete form contains few abandoned subplots or inconsistencies of detail.
questions.explanation: To isolate the writers' pressure, a case must have deadline composition without intermittent reading; C supplies exactly that, and the features it shows (abandoned subplots, inconsistencies) are the ones the fourth paragraph links to writers rather than readers. E is the most tempting trap: it fits the writer-side account, but its novel lacks both deadline composition and intermittent reading, so it cannot tell the two pressures apart. A is a Carrow-like case that isolates the readers' pressure, B is Varga's own undifferentiated comparison, and D concerns readers' needs.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The Orlen Valley ledgers show that rural households of the period lacked the arithmetic needed to reconcile accounts with their neighbors.
Orlen Valley households kept careful accounts with outside merchants because they distrusted merchants more than they distrusted their neighbors.
The persistent imbalances in Orlen Valley accounts between neighbors, once attributed to poor bookkeeping, may instead have been a deliberate means of keeping relationships between households open.
The account between the Brenn and Tamm households shows that disputes between Orlen families were usually caused by the closing of an account.
Parish records demonstrate that whenever an Orlen household repaid a neighbor exactly, a quarrel between the two families followed.
questions.explanation: The passage sets up a puzzle (paragraph 1), presents Halvik's explanation (paragraph 2), and supports it with evidence and an example, concluding that the ledgers may record who remained bound to whom; C captures this, including the author's hedged 'If Halvik is right.' A is the early commentators' view that the passage rejects. D is the most tempting trap: the Brenn account is only an illustration, and it shows the closing coinciding with a quarrel, not causing one, let alone that this was usual; E is too extreme ('whenever') given that the records only 'frequently' note disputes.

questions.stem: In using the phrase “on the long thread” (last sentence of the second paragraph), the ledgers most probably refer to
choices: an account between neighbors that has been deliberately left unsettled so that the obligation between them continues
a debt that has gone unpaid for so long that the creditor has given up hope of repayment
an account kept over many years with a grain merchant from outside the valley
a chain of borrowing in which a single loan passed through many households in turn
a record whose errors were too numerous for the bookkeeper to reconcile
questions.explanation: Halvik cites the expression as the local name for 'such an account', i.e., one in which a small remainder is kept 'perpetually outstanding' to keep the relationship open (paragraph 2); that is A. B is tempting because the account is long-lived, but nothing suggests repayment was hoped for and abandoned; the remainder was intended to stay open. C reverses the evidence, since merchant accounts were closed exactly, and E is the early commentators' reading Halvik rejects.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the accounts that Orlen households kept with grain merchants from outside the valley
choices: were kept less carefully than the households' accounts with their neighbors
were often left with small remainders whose direction alternated over time
were the only ledger entries that archivists catalogued in the 1950s
were closed exactly whenever a transaction was complete
frequently gave rise to disputes that were recorded in parish registers
questions.explanation: The third paragraph states that these accounts 'were closed to the last measure whenever a transaction was complete,' which is D. B attributes the features of neighbors' accounts to merchants' accounts, and A reverses the contrast the passage draws. E transfers the parish-record evidence, which concerns neighbors' accounts that were closed exactly, to the merchant accounts.

questions.stem: If Halvik’s theory is correct, which one of the following would be most likely to have been true of a household that had newly settled in the Orlen Valley during the period in which the ledgers were kept?
choices: It would have avoided borrowing from its neighbors until it had established accounts with outside merchants.
If it wished to establish lasting ties with a neighbor, it would have repaid its first loan from that neighbor with slightly more or slightly less than it had borrowed.
It would have been expected to repay each neighbor exactly until the neighbor had extended it a second loan.
It would have kept its accounts with neighbors in a different measure from the one it used with outside merchants.
It would have been unable to borrow grain from neighbors without first performing labor for them.
questions.explanation: On Halvik's theory, exact repayment signaled a wish to end a relationship and a small outstanding remainder kept it open (paragraph 2), so a newcomer seeking ties would leave a remainder, as in B. C is the attractive trap: it invents a probationary custom of exact repayment that, under Halvik's theory, would signal the opposite of what the newcomer wants. A and E have no basis in the passage, and D borrows the idea of measures without any support.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most call into question Halvik’s theory mentioned in the first sentence of the second paragraph?
choices: Households in a neighboring valley during the same period kept accounts with their neighbors that nearly always balanced exactly.
The Orlen ledgers rarely record the purposes for which grain or tools were borrowed.
Several of the quarrels recorded in Orlen parish registers involved families whose accounts with each other remained open afterward.
Households that kept ledgers in the Orlen Valley tended to be somewhat wealthier than households that did not.

The remainders in accounts between Orlen neighbors closely match the discrepancies produced by converting among the several inconsistent local grain measures then in use, none of which was used in dealings with outside merchants.
questions.explanation: Halvik claims the remainders were deliberate; E supplies a non-deliberate cause that explains both their small size and the contrast with exactly closed merchant accounts, undercutting her strongest evidence. C is the most tempting trap, but Halvik never claims that every quarrel closed an account, only that exact closings frequently coincided with disputes, so open accounts surviving some quarrels barely touches the theory. A concerns a different community, whose customs could differ, and B and D are irrelevant to why the remainders existed.

questions.stem: The passage cites each of the following as evidence supporting Halvik’s theory EXCEPT:
choices: testimony from present-day residents of the valley describing the custom of leaving debts unsettled
the exactness with which accounts with outside merchants were closed
the small size of the remainders carried forward in accounts between neighbors
the tendency of the direction of the imbalance between two households to alternate
the coincidence of exactly closed accounts between neighbors with disputes or departures
questions.explanation: The third paragraph lists the evidence: precise merchant accounts (B), small remainders (C) and alternating imbalances (D), and parish records linking exact closings to disputes or departures (E). Nothing in the passage mentions present-day testimony, so A is the exception. E can look unfamiliar because it paraphrases the 'Finally' sentence, but it is stated there.

questions.stem: The author discusses the ledger of the Brenn household primarily in order to
choices: provide evidence that Orlen households valued labor more highly than grain
illustrate the kind of arithmetic error that early commentators attributed to Orlen bookkeepers
suggest that Halvik's theory applies more clearly to some kinds of loans than to others
show in a single case how alternating imbalances were sustained over many years and how such an account came to be closed
establish that quarrels over boundaries were the most common reason that accounts between neighbors were closed
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph opens by saying the Brenn ledger 'illustrates the mechanism,' then traces the alternating imbalance for thirty-one years and its closing in the year of a quarrel, which is D. A seizes on one detail (labor valued at slightly more than a bushel) that serves only to show the imbalance flipping. E overgeneralizes from a single case, and B is the commentators' interpretation the example is meant to replace.

questions.stem: The information in the passage most helps to answer which one of the following questions?
choices: How many weeks do slate pearlmussel glochidia remain encapsulated on a Halder herring before dropping off?
Why did improvements in water quality above the Ostrow Dam fail to halt the decline of the slate pearlmussel there?
Which fish species other than the Halder herring did Kovač test in the laboratory?
How much did the fish lift at the Ostrow Dam cost to build and operate?
Why do slate pearlmussels live longer than most other freshwater mussels?
questions.explanation: The passage explains that the dam ended the herring runs on which glochidia depend, so the upstream population could not reproduce whatever the water quality (paragraph 2), answering B. A is the tempting trap, but the passage says only 'several weeks,' not a specific number. C, D, and E concern information the passage never gives; it says adults live long but not why, or how that compares with other mussels.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the conclusions Kovač drew in 1994 (second paragraph)?
choices: Adult slate pearlmussels upstream of the dam grow more slowly than those downstream, so that their growth rings are harder to count.
Glochidia of several other mussel species in the Halder River transform successfully on many different fish species.
Halder herring tolerate polluted water better than most other fish species in the river do.
Juvenile mussels of many species are more sensitive to fine sediment than biologists believed in 1994.
In a tributary that joins the Halder above the dam and whose bed has remained free of fine sediment, the slate pearlmussels are likewise nearly all more than sixty years old.
questions.explanation: Kovač's critics proposed sediment above the dam as an alternative explanation for the missing age classes (paragraph 3); E shows the same age gap where there is no sediment but herring are still blocked, ruling out that alternative. D strengthens the critics rather than Kovač, and A casts doubt on her aging method. B concerns other species, and C is irrelevant to whether the herring's absence prevents reproduction.

questions.stem: The information yielded by which one of the following experiments would be most useful in determining whether the critics described in the third paragraph were correct that the missing age classes reflected where juveniles could survive?
choices: exposing slate pearlmussel glochidia in the laboratory to additional fish species found above the dam
counting the growth rings of slate pearlmussels collected from several sites below the dam
placing juvenile pearlmussels raised on herring in a hatchery into cages on the riverbed above the dam and monitoring their survival
comparing the number of glochidia released by female pearlmussels above the dam with the number released by females below it
measuring concentrations of industrial pollutants in the water above the dam during the herring's former spawning season
questions.explanation: The sediment critics claimed juveniles could not survive above the dam even if produced; C supplies juveniles directly and tests their survival in that riverbed, isolating survival from production. A is the strongest trap, but it tests the other objection (whether hosts in the wild differ from those in tanks), not the sediment claim. D measures larval output, which bears on production rather than juvenile survival, and B and E do not involve the upstream riverbed's effect on juveniles.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the passage?
choices: Before Kovač's work, the decline of the slate pearlmussel above the Ostrow Dam had been attributed mainly to the condition of the river's water and bed.
Kovač believed that the water-quality measures begun in 1978 had harmed the slate pearlmussel.
Adult slate pearlmussels are more sensitive to fine sediment than juveniles are.
Halder herring no longer spawn anywhere in the Halder River.
The fish lift at the Ostrow Dam was built in direct response to Kovač's laboratory findings.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says the decline was attributed to industrial pollution and agricultural sediment, which is the condition of the water and the bed, so A is supported. B is too strong: Kovač wanted funds redirected, not because the measures did harm but because they did not address the problem. C reverses the passage's claim about juveniles, D goes beyond it (the herring may still spawn below the dam), and E asserts a causal link the passage never draws, since the lift came fourteen years later after resistance.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following about the surveys of the 1970s mentioned in the first paragraph?
choices: They overstated the extent of the decline, since many old mussels above the dam were still alive.
Their findings were inconsistent with the view that pollution was responsible for the decline.
They should have led biologists to examine the mussel's life cycle rather than the river's water quality.
The decline they recorded would not by itself have revealed that the population above the dam had ceased to reproduce.
They counted mussels below the dam as well as above it, which obscured the difference between the two populations.
questions.explanation: The surveys recorded falling numbers; Kovač's insight required aging the mussels, since a population of long-lived adults that has stopped reproducing appears 'merely diminished' (paragraph 2) and 'can conceal a failure of reproduction' (paragraph 4), which supports D. B is the most tempting trap, but a decline in numbers is perfectly consistent with a pollution explanation, which is why it was accepted. C imports a normative judgment the author never makes about the surveys, and A and E lack support.

questions.stem: The author mentions that recruitment was markedly lower in the siltiest reaches (middle of the last paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: suggest that the fish lift has failed to restore reproduction in most of the river above the dam
acknowledge that one objection to Kovač's account identified a genuine factor even though it did not explain the absence of young mussels
show that Kovač's critics were correct that the missing age classes reflected where juveniles could survive
argue that funding for water-quality measures above the dam should be restored
cast doubt on Kovač's laboratory findings about which fish could serve as hosts
questions.explanation: The sentence concedes that the sediment critics 'had identified a real, though secondary, constraint,' after the passage has shown juveniles appearing even where sediment had not changed; that is B. C is the trap: it takes the concession too far, since recruitment resumed once herring returned, showing that host absence, not sediment, explained the missing age classes. A exaggerates 'lower' into failure, and D and E are not suggested.

questions.stimulus: Coach: Our league should not adopt the proposed rule limiting youth pitchers to forty pitches per game. The rule's supporters say it will reduce arm injuries, and that is a worthy aim. But most arm injuries among our players occur during off-season travel tournaments, which the league does not govern. So a pitch limit in league games would do little to protect players' arms.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the conclusion drawn in the coach's argument?
choices: Reducing arm injuries among youth pitchers is a worthy aim.
Most arm injuries among the league's players occur during off-season travel tournaments.
The league should not adopt the proposed forty-pitch limit for youth pitchers.
A pitch limit in league games would do little to protect players' arms.
The league should begin to govern off-season travel tournaments.
questions.explanation: The coach's point is the opening claim that the league should not adopt the pitch limit; everything else supports it, so C is correct. D is the tempting trap: it is itself supported by the claim about travel tournaments, but it is offered as the reason for rejecting the rule, making it an intermediate conclusion. A is a concession and E is never proposed.

questions.stimulus: Owner of Kessel's Bakery: In March we began setting out free samples of our pastries on the counter, and our pastry sales in March were 15 percent higher than in February. So offering free samples is an effective way to increase our pastry sales, and we should keep doing it.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: overlooks the possibility that something other than the samples accounts for the rise in March sales
presumes that customers who tried a sample bought only the kind of pastry they sampled
fails to establish that the rise in pastry sales increased the bakery's overall profits
takes for granted that what works for one bakery will work for every bakery
treats the owner's own taste in pastries as representative of the customers' tastes
questions.explanation: The owner infers that the samples caused the March increase merely because the increase followed them; a seasonal shift or some other change could explain it, so A is correct. C is tempting, but the conclusion is only about increasing pastry sales, not profits. The argument never generalizes beyond this bakery (D) or relies on the owner's taste (E).

questions.stimulus: Gardener: This summer the tomato plants in my plot, which I mulched with straw, produced far fewer split fruits than the unmulched tomato plants in my neighbor's plot. Tomatoes split when soil moisture swings sharply, and straw mulch keeps soil moisture steady. So mulching with straw reduces fruit splitting in tomatoes.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the gardener's argument?
choices: Straw mulch also suppresses weeds that compete with tomato plants for nutrients.
Some tomato varieties are much more prone to splitting than others are.
The gardener's neighbor harvested more tomatoes in total this summer than the gardener did.
The few tomato plants in the gardener's own plot that were left unmulched split about as often as the neighbor's plants did.
Tomato splitting tends to be more common in years with heavy late-summer rain.
questions.explanation: The comparison is between two different plots, so some difference other than mulch (variety, watering, soil) could explain the result. D shows that unmulched plants in the gardener's own plot split as often as the neighbor's, isolating mulch as the relevant difference. B is tempting but only raises a possible alternative cause without saying the plots differed in variety, so it if anything weakens; E affects both plots alike.

questions.stimulus: Striped grunters, a reef fish found off Varrow Island, feed mostly at night, when they are most active. Yet divers who survey the reef during the day count far more striped grunters than divers who survey it at night.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why divers count more striped grunters by day than by night?
choices: Striped grunters are preyed upon by several species of eels that hunt at night.
At night striped grunters scatter singly across distant seagrass beds to feed, but by day they rest in large schools directly over the reef.
Divers surveying the reef at night carry powerful lights that make fish visible at a distance.
The striped grunter is among the most abundant fish species on the reef.
Many other fish species found near Varrow Island also feed mostly at night.
questions.explanation: One would expect a fish active at night to be easier to find at night. B explains the pattern: by day the grunters gather in plain view over the reef that divers survey, while at night they disperse away from it. C deepens the puzzle, and A does not explain why the fish would be seen more often by day.

questions.stimulus: Health official: The rate of hospitalization for childhood asthma in Tarrow County is twice that in neighboring Ellis County. The air in Tarrow contains far more diesel exhaust than Ellis's air does, mostly from Tarrow's freight yards. Therefore, reducing diesel exhaust in Tarrow would lower its rate of hospitalization for childhood asthma.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the health official's argument?
choices: Diesel exhaust is the primary cause of childhood asthma in Tarrow County.
Ellis County has no freight yards or other major sources of diesel exhaust.
Reducing diesel exhaust in Tarrow County would also lower the rate of respiratory illness among adults there.
Children in Tarrow County with asthma attacks are more likely than those in Ellis County to be taken to a hospital.
Exposure to diesel exhaust can contribute to children's asthma becoming severe enough to require hospitalization.
questions.explanation: If diesel exhaust could not worsen children's asthma to the point of hospitalization, cutting it would do nothing to the hospitalization rate, so the argument requires E. A is the tempting trap but is too strong: exhaust need only be one contributing factor, not the primary cause of asthma. B is not needed (Ellis need only have less exhaust), and D would weaken the argument.

questions.stimulus:
Rosa: The Marlton city orchestra should devote nearly all of its programs to established classical works. Those works draw the largest audiences, and ticket sales are what keep the orchestra solvent.

Malik: Ticket sales certainly matter. But an orchestra that plays only familiar works will gradually lose younger listeners, who are its future audience. The orchestra should give a substantial share of its programs to new compositions.
questions.stem: Rosa and Malik disagree over whether
choices: ticket sales are important to the orchestra's financial health
established classical works draw larger audiences than new compositions do
the orchestra should devote nearly all of its programs to established classical works
younger listeners prefer new compositions to established classical works
the orchestra is currently in financial difficulty
questions.explanation: Rosa says nearly all programs should be established works; Malik says a substantial share should be new compositions, which rules out 'nearly all,' so they disagree about C. Malik concedes that ticket sales matter (A) and never disputes that classics draw larger audiences (B). Rosa says nothing about younger listeners' preferences (D), and neither says the orchestra is in difficulty (E).

questions.stimulus: Transit planner: Since the city raised the fare on Route 9 buses from $1.50 to $2.00 last year, Route 9 ridership has fallen by a third. To win back those riders, we should return the fare to $1.50.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the transit planner's argument?
choices: Shortly after the fare increase, a new light-rail line opened along most of Route 9's path, and many former Route 9 riders now use it.
Ridership on several of the city's other bus routes also fell after the fare increase.
Even at $2.00, the Route 9 fare is lower than bus fares in most comparable cities.
Returning the fare to $1.50 would reduce the transit system's revenue per rider.
Some Route 9 riders have complained about crowded buses during rush hour.
questions.explanation: The planner assumes the fare increase drove riders away, so lowering the fare would bring them back. A offers another cause of the decline, a competing rail line, which a fare cut would not undo. B tends to support the fare explanation, and C and D are about comparisons and revenue rather than about why riders left.

questions.stimulus: In Darrow County, defendants awaiting trial who cannot afford bail remain in jail. A study of the county's criminal cases found that defendants held in jail before trial were more likely to plead guilty than were released defendants facing similar charges and comparably strong evidence. Many of the jailed defendants who pleaded guilty were sentenced to the time they had already served.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Most defendants in Darrow County who plead guilty are in fact innocent.
Defendants in Darrow County who are released before trial are less likely to be convicted at trial.
Bail amounts in Darrow County are higher than those in most other counties.
In Darrow County, some defendants' decisions to plead guilty are influenced by factors other than the strength of the evidence against them.
Eliminating bail in Darrow County would cut the number of guilty pleas there roughly in half.
questions.explanation: Jailed and released defendants with comparably strong evidence pleaded guilty at different rates, so something besides the evidence, such as being jailed, affects some decisions to plead; D follows. A is the tempting overreach: the facts show pleas are influenced by detention, not that most who plead are innocent. B, C, and E introduce trials, other counties, and a specific number the facts do not address.

questions.stimulus: Agronomist: Any field planted with winter rye after the harvest will lose less soil to erosion over the winter than it otherwise would. All of the Hollis farm's fields will be planted with winter rye after this fall's harvest. So the Hollis farm will qualify for the county's soil-conservation grant.
questions.stem: The agronomist's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Only farms that plant winter rye on all of their fields qualify for the county's soil-conservation grant.
Any farm all of whose fields will lose less soil to erosion over the winter than they otherwise would qualifies for the county's soil-conservation grant.
Every farm that qualifies for the county's soil-conservation grant loses less soil to erosion over the winter than it otherwise would.
Most farms that plant winter rye after the harvest qualify for the county's soil-conservation grant.
Winter rye reduces winter soil erosion more than any other crop that can be planted after the harvest.
questions.explanation: The premises establish that every Hollis field will lose less soil over the winter; B makes exactly that a sufficient condition for the grant, so the conclusion follows. A is the attractive trap, but 'only' gives a necessary condition for qualifying, not a guarantee. C reverses the needed conditional, and D's 'most' cannot guarantee that this particular farm qualifies.

questions.stimulus: Sportswriter: Each of the five starters on the Harbor City basketball team was chosen for the regional all-star squad last season. So the Harbor City team must have been the best team in the region last season.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: relies on the judgment of all-star selectors who may know little about how well players work together
takes for granted that the regional all-star squad included players from every team in the region
takes for granted that players were chosen as all-stars solely for their scoring
draws a conclusion about every season from evidence about a single season
presumes that a team whose individual starters are outstanding must itself be outstanding as a team
questions.explanation: The sportswriter moves from the excellence of each starter to the excellence of the team as a whole, though a team of strong individuals can still play poorly together; E describes this. A is tempting because it mentions teamwork, but the argument's problem is not reliance on the selectors' judgment of individuals, which may be sound. The conclusion concerns only last season (D), and nothing presumes all-stars were chosen for scoring (C).

questions.stimulus: Dr. Imani: Some residents want the city to stop fluoridating its water because a few people have reported mild tooth discoloration. But by that standard, the city would also have to stop chlorinating the water, since chlorine sometimes gives water an unpleasant taste. No one seriously proposes ending chlorination, which protects against waterborne disease. So mild discoloration alone is not a good reason to end fluoridation.
questions.stem: Dr. Imani's argument proceeds by
choices: showing that the reasoning behind a proposal would, if applied consistently, support a conclusion that is clearly unacceptable
offering evidence that the reported tooth discoloration was not in fact caused by fluoridation
arguing that the benefits of fluoridation are greater than the benefits of chlorination
questioning the motives of the residents who reported tooth discoloration
citing expert opinion to establish that fluoridation poses no health risks
questions.explanation: Dr. Imani argues that the residents' standard (a minor side effect justifies ending a treatment) would also require ending chlorination, an absurd result, so A is correct. B is tempting because it seems a natural rebuttal, but Dr. Imani never disputes that fluoridation caused the discoloration. She does not rank the benefits of the two treatments (C), attack motives (D), or cite experts (E).

questions.stimulus: Dunmore Hardware policy: An employee may approve a customer refund only if the employee has completed the store's register training. Every employee who works weekend shifts has completed register training. Jalen, a Dunmore Hardware employee, has not completed register training.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Every Dunmore Hardware employee who has completed register training may approve refunds.
Every Dunmore Hardware employee who may approve refunds works weekend shifts.
Jalen does not work weekend shifts at Dunmore Hardware.
Some Dunmore Hardware employees who have not completed register training work weekend shifts.
Jalen will complete register training before he is assigned any weekend shifts.
questions.explanation: Working weekends guarantees completed training, so by the contrapositive anyone without the training, including Jalen, does not work weekends; C must be true. A reverses the first rule, treating a necessary condition as sufficient. B does not follow, because trained employees who approve refunds might work only weekdays, and D contradicts the second rule.

questions.stimulus: Marine biologist: Five years ago, bottom trawling was banned in Selby Bay. Since then, the number of juvenile cod counted in the bay's annual survey has tripled. Evidently, the ban has allowed the bay's cod population to recover.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions most helps in evaluating the marine biologist's argument?
choices: Does bottom trawling also harm fish species other than cod?
Was the trawling ban supported by most of the bay's commercial fishing crews?
Has the cost of enforcing the ban exceeded the original estimates?
Was bottom trawling banned in Selby Bay before it was banned in other bays in the region?
Did juvenile cod counts rise by a similar amount over the same period in nearby waters where bottom trawling continued?
questions.explanation: The argument credits the ban with the rise in juvenile cod, but a regionwide trend could explain it. If counts rose just as much where trawling continued, the ban looks irrelevant; if not, the ban is better supported, so E matters. A and D are on topic but do not bear on whether the ban caused this rise, and B and C concern politics and cost.

questions.stimulus: Prosecutors should offer a defendant a reduced charge in exchange for a guilty plea only if the defendant has no prior conviction for a violent offense and, in any case with an identifiable victim, the victim has been told of the proposed offer.
questions.stem: The principle stated above most helps to justify the reasoning in which one of the following arguments?
choices: Ortiz has no prior convictions, and the victim of his theft has been told of the proposed offer. So the prosecutor should offer Ortiz a reduced charge in exchange for a guilty plea.
Hale has no prior convictions of any kind, but the owner of the shop Hale vandalized has not been told of the proposed offer. So the prosecutor should not yet offer Hale a reduced charge.
Pryce has a prior conviction for fraud, which is not a violent offense. So the prosecutor should not offer Pryce a reduced charge in exchange for a guilty plea.
Lam's offense had no identifiable victim, though Lam has a prior conviction for assault. So the prosecutor may offer Lam a reduced charge once the community has been consulted.
The victim of Reyes's burglary was told of the proposed offer and objected to it. So the prosecutor should not offer Reyes a reduced charge in exchange for a guilty plea.
questions.explanation: The principle states only necessary conditions, so it can justify only a conclusion that an offer should not be made when a condition fails. In B the shop owner, an identifiable victim, has not been told, so the offer should not be made yet. A is the main trap: both conditions are met, but meeting necessary conditions does not show the offer should be made. E is also tempting, but the principle requires only that the victim be told, not that the victim agree, and C misapplies it because fraud is not a violent offense.

questions.stimulus: City engineer: At the intersections where we replaced four-way stop signs with small traffic circles, collisions fell by 40 percent the following year. Drivers must slow down to get through a traffic circle, and slower speeds mean fewer collisions. So we should install traffic circles at the city's remaining four-way-stop intersections as well.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the city engineer's argument?
choices: Traffic circles cost less to maintain than traffic signals do.
Many drivers say they find traffic circles confusing the first time they encounter them.
In the year before the conversion, the converted intersections had more collisions than any other intersections in the city.
The intersections that were converted were chosen at random from among all of the city's four-way-stop intersections.
Some of the collisions at the converted intersections in the following year involved pedestrians.
questions.explanation: The engineer generalizes from the converted intersections to the rest. If those intersections were picked at random (D), they are representative of the remaining ones, and an unusual year at specially chosen sites is less likely to explain the drop. C is the trap: it actually weakens the argument, because intersections chosen for their unusually bad record would tend to improve anyway and may differ from the rest. A compares circles with signals, which is not the alternative under discussion.

questions.stimulus: After farmers in the Kell Valley switched from flooding their orchards to drip irrigation, they used about 30 percent less water per acre. Yet the total amount of water drawn from the valley's aquifer for agriculture rose in the years after drip irrigation became widespread.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why agricultural water use in the Kell Valley rose?
choices: Drip irrigation made it profitable to grow orchards on hilly land that could not be flood-irrigated, so many farmers greatly expanded their irrigated acreage.
Drip irrigation systems cost more to install than flood irrigation systems do.
A few farmers in the valley continued to flood their orchards after drip irrigation became widespread.
The amount of water drawn from the aquifer by households in the valley also rose during those years.
Drip irrigation reduces the amount of irrigation water lost to evaporation.
questions.explanation: Less water per acre can still mean more water in total if many more acres are irrigated; A supplies exactly that increase in acreage. C is tempting, but holdouts who kept flooding would only limit the savings, not produce a rise above earlier levels. D concerns household rather than agricultural use, and E explains only the per-acre savings.

questions.stimulus: Music teacher: Students who practice an instrument in many short sessions each week generally improve faster than students who practice for the same total time in a few long sessions. Yet most of my students prefer a few long sessions, because those are easier to fit into their schedules.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the music teacher's statements?
choices: Students who practice in a few long sessions each week do not improve.
Most of the teacher's students improve more slowly than the students of other music teachers.
A student's schedule is the most important factor in how quickly that student improves.
The teacher should require students to practice in short sessions.
Some of the teacher's students would probably improve faster if they practiced for the same total time in more frequent, shorter sessions.
questions.explanation: Since short sessions generally produce faster improvement at the same total time, and most of the teacher's students use long sessions, some of them would probably improve faster by switching; E is appropriately hedged. A is too strong, since long sessions only produce slower improvement. D is tempting but recommends a policy the statements never address, and B compares students with other teachers' students.

questions.stimulus: Every swimmer on the Ridgefield club who breaks a club record during the season is invited to the regional training camp. Odile, a Ridgefield swimmer, was invited to the regional training camp this year. So Odile must have broken a club record this season.
questions.stem: The pattern of questionable reasoning in the argument above is most similar to that in which one of the following?
choices: Every chef who trains at the Marlow Institute learns to make stock from scratch. Petra did not train at the Marlow Institute, so she must not have learned to make stock from scratch.
Every apartment in the Elgin Building has a balcony. Dev's apartment has no balcony, so it must not be in the Elgin Building.
Every customer who spends more than $100 at Fenwick's receives a discount coupon. Yusuf received a discount coupon from Fenwick's, so he must have spent more than $100 there.
Only students who pass the entrance exam are admitted to Carlow Academy. Lena was admitted to Carlow Academy, so she must have passed the entrance exam.
Most volunteers who attend the orientation stay with the program for a full year. Malik attended the orientation, so he will probably stay for a full year.
questions.explanation: The argument treats a sufficient condition (breaking a record guarantees an invitation) as if it were necessary, inferring the record from the invitation. C makes the same error, inferring big spending from the coupon, since coupons may be given for other reasons. D looks identical on the surface but is valid, because 'only' makes passing the exam necessary for admission. A commits a different error (denying the antecedent), and B and E are reasonable.

questions.stimulus: Consultant: Coffee shops in Brayton that offer free wireless internet have, on average, higher daily revenue than Brayton coffee shops that do not. So the Corner Cup, a Brayton coffee shop that does not offer wireless internet, would increase its daily revenue by offering it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the consultant's argument?
choices: Offering free wireless internet costs a coffee shop relatively little each month.
Most of the Brayton shops that now offer free wireless internet already had higher daily revenue than other Brayton shops before they began offering it.
Several regular customers of the Corner Cup have asked its owner to offer wireless internet.
Coffee shops in nearby towns that offer free wireless internet also tend to have higher revenue than those that do not.
Some Brayton coffee shops that offer free wireless internet have lower daily revenue than the Corner Cup does.
questions.explanation: The consultant infers from a correlation that wireless internet raises revenue. B shows the revenue gap existed before the service was offered, suggesting that busier shops tend to adopt wireless rather than wireless making shops busier. E is the trap: a comparison of averages allows some wireless shops to earn less, so E does nothing to undercut the claim that wireless raises revenue. C and D tend to support the argument.

questions.stimulus: Ecologist: Sea otters, absent from Calder Sound for decades, returned there twelve years ago. Otters eat sea urchins, and sea urchins graze on kelp. Since the otters' return, the sound's kelp forests have more than doubled in area. Thus, the otters' return is probably the main reason for the expansion of the kelp forests.
questions.stem: The ecologist's argument requires assuming which one of the following?
choices: Sea otters eat more sea urchins than any other predator in Calder Sound does.
Water temperatures in Calder Sound have not changed during the past twelve years.
Expanded kelp forests provide sea otters with shelter from their own predators.
Before the otters returned, sea urchins in Calder Sound were numerous enough to limit the growth of its kelp forests.
Sea urchins in Calder Sound eat no food other than kelp.
questions.explanation: The argument's mechanism is that otters reduce urchins, and fewer urchins let kelp grow. If urchins were too few before the otters returned to hold the kelp back (the negation of D), removing some of them could not explain the expansion. B is tempting, but a temperature change need not have affected kelp, so the argument does not require that temperatures stayed constant. A and E are stronger than the argument needs.

questions.stimulus: Public health director: Of the Fallon County residents who were treated for heat stroke last summer, 70 percent were over age 65. So residents of Fallon County who are over 65 are much more likely to suffer heat stroke than are younger residents.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the public health director's reasoning?
choices: It presumes, without justification, that heat stroke is more dangerous for older residents than for younger ones.
It treats a factor that makes heat stroke more likely as though it were the only cause of heat stroke.
It fails to consider that some younger residents who suffered heat stroke may also have had other illnesses.
It confuses the claim that most heat stroke patients are over 65 with the claim that most residents over 65 suffer heat stroke.
It fails to consider what proportion of Fallon County's residents are over age 65.
questions.explanation: That 70 percent of patients were over 65 shows greater risk only if older people make up much less than 70 percent of the population; if most residents are over 65, the figure is unremarkable. E names this missing base rate. D is the tempting trap: it describes a real confusion, but the director never concludes that most older residents get heat stroke, only that they are more likely to than younger residents. Nothing in the argument concerns danger (A) or a sole cause (B).

questions.stimulus: Legal scholar: A court ruling deserves public confidence only if it is explained in terms that ordinary citizens can follow. But any ruling that turns on a dispute among specialists cannot be explained in such terms unless the court sets out the specialists' competing views in plain language. In the Marsh case, the appellate court's opinion did not set out in plain language the views of either side's forensic experts. So the court's ruling in the Marsh case does not deserve public confidence.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the legal scholar's argument can be properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: The appellate court's ruling in the Marsh case turned on a dispute between the two sides' forensic experts.
Any court ruling that sets out specialists' competing views in plain language is explained in terms that ordinary citizens can follow.
A court ruling that is explained in terms that ordinary citizens can follow deserves public confidence.
Most court rulings that turn on a dispute among specialists fail to set out the specialists' views in plain language.
The forensic experts in the Marsh case disagreed with each other about matters that ordinary citizens could not follow.
questions.explanation: The second rule applies only to rulings that turn on a dispute among specialists. If the Marsh ruling did (A), then because the experts' views were not set out plainly, the ruling was not explained in followable terms, and by the first rule it does not deserve confidence. E is the most attractive trap: it says the experts disagreed, but not that the ruling turned on their dispute, so the second rule still is not triggered. B and C reverse the stated conditionals, and D's 'most' says nothing about this case.

questions.stimulus: Most commuters in Pell City choose between driving downtown and taking the train mainly on the basis of total travel time. The city plans to add express trains that would cut the train trip downtown by ten minutes. But the city also plans to close two of the three parking lots at the Maple Street station, where most train commuters board after driving there. Unless commuters can find parking quickly elsewhere, the time saved on the train may be lost searching for a space. So ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: the city should cancel its plan to close the parking lots at the Maple Street station
adding express trains may not, by itself, make the train more attractive to commuters than it is now
the number of commuters who take the train will decline once the parking lots are closed
commuters care more about the availability of parking than about total travel time
most commuters who now drive downtown would switch to the train if parking at the station were expanded
questions.explanation: Commuters weigh total travel time, and the ten minutes saved on the train may be lost hunting for parking, so the express trains may fail to make the train more attractive; B matches the argument's cautious 'may.' C is the tempting trap but is too strong: the argument says only that the savings may be lost, not that ridership will fall. A draws a policy recommendation the argument does not reach, and D contradicts the first sentence.

questions.stimulus: Museum director: The Halvorsen Museum should not lend its fragile, one-of-a-kind medieval tapestry to the touring exhibition, even though the tour would let many thousands of people see the tapestry who otherwise never would. Each move exposes the tapestry to a small but real risk of irreparable damage, and once it is damaged, no future visitor will ever see it as it is now.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the museum director's argument?
choices: A museum should lend its works only to exhibitions organized by institutions with expertise in conservation.
Museums should make the works in their collections accessible to as many people as possible.
A museum should not lend a work if the work could be damaged by conditions in the borrowing institution's galleries.
A museum should not subject an irreplaceable work to any risk of permanent damage solely in order to let more people see it.
The risk of damage to a work of art should be weighed against the educational benefit of showing it to new audiences.
questions.explanation: The director concedes the tour's benefit, wider viewing, but holds that a small risk of irreparable damage to a unique work outweighs it. D states that principle exactly, so the conclusion follows. E is the attractive trap: it describes weighing risk against benefit, but it does not say which way the balance comes out, so it cannot justify refusing the loan. C concerns the borrower's galleries, while the director's concern is the moves themselves, and B supports lending.

questions.stimulus: Most of the orchards in the Daltry region that were sprayed with kaolin clay last season suffered little sunburn damage to their fruit. Every orchard in the region that suffered little sunburn damage got a premium price for its apples. So some of the orchards in the region that were sprayed with kaolin clay got a premium price for their apples.
questions.stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following arguments is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Most of the musicians in the Fairview orchestra studied at a conservatory. Most musicians who studied at a conservatory can sight-read difficult scores. So some musicians in the Fairview orchestra can sight-read difficult scores.
Every bicycle sold at Corliss Cycles comes with a one-year warranty. Most bicycles with a one-year warranty are made overseas. So some bicycles sold at Corliss Cycles are made overseas.

Most of the restaurants that passed the city's health inspection last month had also been inspected the previous year. Every restaurant inspected the previous year was sent a reminder notice. So some restaurants that passed last month's inspection were sent a reminder notice.

Most of the novels on this year's prize shortlist were written by first-time authors. Some first-time authors have received writing grants. So some novels on the shortlist were written by authors who received writing grants.
Every greenhouse at the Ames nursery is heated by solar panels. No greenhouse heated by solar panels needs a backup generator. So no greenhouse at the Ames nursery needs a backup generator.
questions.explanation: The argument is valid: most A are B, every B is C, so some A are C. C has exactly this form (most restaurants that passed were inspected the year before; every one inspected then got a notice; so some that passed got a notice). A is the most tempting trap because it also concludes 'some,' but its second premise says 'most' rather than 'every,' and two 'most' statements need not overlap, so it is invalid. B and D are likewise invalid, and E is valid but has a different, all-and-none form.
